tips.title: Two formulae, both given in the specification
tips.body: Image: **size in bits = W × H × D**. Sound: **size in bits = rate × res × secs**. Both give **bits**, so divide by **8** for bytes. Learn them as multiplications of everything involved and neither can be muddled.

tips.title: Colour depth is bits, not colours
tips.body: **D is the number of bits per pixel.** The number of **colours** is $2^D$: 1 bit gives 2, 2 bits give 4, 8 bits give 256. Questions swap the two deliberately, so read which is being asked for.

tips.title: The answer is in bits until you divide
tips.body: Both formulae produce **bits**. A question asking for **bytes** needs ÷ 8, and one asking for **kB** needs ÷ 8 ÷ 1000. Forgetting the divide is the single most common way to lose the last mark here.

tips.title: Every factor is linear
tips.body: Double the sampling rate, or the resolution, or the seconds, and the file **doubles**. Double an image's width **and** height and it goes up **four** times, because both dimensions are in the formula.

tips.title: A sample is an amplitude at a point in time
tips.body: The specification's wording: a sample is **a measure of amplitude at a point in time**. Sampling **rate** is how many are taken each second, in hertz; sample **resolution** is how many **bits** each one uses.

steps.title: Bitmap images
steps.body:
**A pixel is a picture element** — short for exactly that — and it is a **single point** in an image. A bitmap image is a grid of them, and the computer stores a binary code for each one saying what colour it is.

Zoom far enough into any photograph and the squares appear. There is nothing else in a bitmap: no lines, no shapes, just the colour of every point.

**Two properties describe a bitmap:**

**Image size** is measured in **pixels**, written **width × height**. A 100 × 50 image is 100 pixels across and 50 down, so it holds 5000 pixels altogether.

**Colour depth** is the number of **bits used to represent each pixel**. This is the one that gets misread: it is a count of **bits**, not of colours. The number of colours available is $2^D$:

| Colour depth | Colours available |
| --- | --- |
| 1 bit | $2^1 = $ **2** |
| 2 bits | $2^2 = $ **4** |
| 8 bits | $2^8 = $ **256** |
| 24 bits | $2^{24} = $ **16,777,216** |

**Both affect the file size**, because every pixel is stored and every pixel takes the same number of bits. More pixels means more of them to store; a greater colour depth means each one costs more.

**And both affect quality.** More pixels give more detail — too few and the image looks blocky. A greater colour depth allows finer shading — too little and smooth gradients turn into visible bands.

steps.title: Calculating an image file size
steps.body:
**The formula is given in the specification:**

$$\text{Size (bits)} = W \times H \times D$$
$$\text{Size (bytes)} = \frac{W \times H \times D}{8}$$

where $W$ is the width, $H$ the height and $D$ the colour depth in bits.

steps.title: Binary and the picture
steps.body:
**You may be given a bit pattern and asked to draw the image, or given an image and asked to write the pattern.**

With a colour depth of **1 bit**, each pixel is a single 0 or 1 — two colours, so say black and white. The bits are read **across each row in turn**, top row first.

This 4 × 4 pattern:

`1001` `0110` `0110` `1001`

reads as four rows of four pixels. Taking **1 as black**, the black pixels sit at the four corners and at the four middle squares — a cross from corner to corner.

**Check the count.** 4 × 4 × 1 = **16 bits**, and the pattern has exactly 16 digits. If your pattern is longer or shorter than $W \times H \times D$, you have mis-read the width.

**Going the other way** is the same process reversed: take the top row, write a bit for each pixel, then the next row, and so on. The width has to be known — the same 16 bits would make a completely different picture as 2 × 8 or 8 × 2.

**Which value means which colour is a convention**, and a question will tell you. Do not assume 1 is black; read the key given.

steps.title: Representing sound
steps.body:
**Sound is analogue.** A real sound wave varies **continuously** — it has a value at every instant, and those values change smoothly. A computer can only store **discrete** numbers, so the wave must be converted to a digital form before it can be stored or processed.

**That conversion is called sampling.** The wave's height is measured at regular intervals and each measurement is stored as a binary number. The specification defines a **sample** as **a measure of amplitude at a point in time**.

**Two properties describe the result:**

**Sampling rate** is the **number of samples taken in a second**, measured in **hertz** — 1 hertz is 1 sample per second. A rate of 8,000 Hz takes 8,000 measurements every second.

**Sample resolution** is the **number of bits per sample**. More bits means each measurement can be recorded more precisely.

**Both affect quality and file size.** A higher rate captures more of the wave's shape, so the digital version follows the original more closely. A higher resolution records each height more exactly. Both mean more data.

**The formula, again from the specification:**

$$\text{File size (bits)} = \text{rate} \times \text{res} \times \text{secs}$$

**Worked:** 8,000 Hz at 8-bit resolution for 10 seconds is 8,000 × 8 × 10 = **640,000 bits**, which is 80,000 bytes, or **80 kB**.

**The digital version is never exact.** Between two samples the computer has no record of what the wave did, so some of the original is always lost. More samples make the approximation closer, never perfect.

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**Write the formula before the numbers.** $W \times H \times D$ and $\text{rate} \times \text{res} \times \text{secs}$. Both are given in the specification, both are plain multiplications, and writing them first earns the method mark even if the arithmetic then slips.

**Both formulae give bits.** Check the unit the question asks for. Bytes needs ÷ 8; kilobytes needs ÷ 8 then ÷ 1000. A right number in the wrong unit loses the final mark, and this is the most common way it goes here.

**Colour depth is bits per pixel, and $2^D$ is the number of colours.** A question may give you either and ask for the other. If a question says "256 colours", the depth to put in the formula is **8**, not 256 — substituting 256 is a large and very visible error.

**Reason about changes rather than recalculating.** Every factor is **linear**: double the rate, the resolution or the duration and the file doubles. For an image, doubling **both** width and height multiplies the size by **four**, because both appear in the formula. Saying "four times, because both dimensions doubled" is a better answer than a page of arithmetic.

**Use the specification's wording for a sample**: *a measure of amplitude at a point in time*. Not "a bit of the sound".

**Explain why digital sound is approximate.** The original wave is **continuous** — it has a value at every instant. Sampling records it only at **intervals**, and between two samples nothing is stored. The digital version is therefore always an approximation; a higher rate makes it closer but never exact. That reasoning is what an "explain" question is looking for, rather than "it loses quality".

**Know the width before drawing a bitmap.** The same bits make a different picture at a different width, and the bit count must equal $W \times H \times D$ — a free check on whether you have read the pattern correctly.

**Do not invent extra terms.** The specification says to use **only** colour depth and the number of pixels. Adding an allowance for a file header is not wanted here and will not match the mark scheme.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- A **pixel** is short for **picture element** — a single point in an image.
- **Image size** is in pixels, written **width × height**.
- **Colour depth** is the number of **bits per pixel**.
- The number of colours available is **$2^D$**: 1 bit gives 2, 8 bits give 256.
- **Size (bits) = W × H × D**; **Size (bytes) = W × H × D ÷ 8**.
- More pixels or greater depth means a **larger file** and **better quality**.
- Doubling **both** dimensions multiplies file size by **four**.
- A 1-bit bitmap is read **across each row in turn**; the bit count must equal $W \times H \times D$.
- **Sound is analogue** — continuous — and must be converted to digital.
- That conversion is **sampling**.
- A **sample** is a **measure of amplitude at a point in time**.
- **Sampling rate** is samples per second, in **hertz**.
- **Sample resolution** is the number of **bits per sample**.
- **File size (bits) = rate × res × secs**.
- Nothing is recorded **between** samples, so digital sound is always an **approximation**.

questions.prompt: The word pixel is short for which two words?
questions.solution: **Picture element**. A pixel is a single point in an image.

questions.prompt: How is the size of a bitmap image measured?
options: In pixels, as width × height
In bytes, as width + height
In centimetres across the screen
In the number of colours it uses
questions.solution: Image size is measured **in pixels**, using the notation **width × height**.

questions.prompt: An image is 20 pixels wide and 10 pixels high with a colour depth of 4 bits. What is its file size in bits?
How many colours can be represented with a colour depth of 4 bits?
questions.solution: $2^4 = $ **16** colours. The depth is 4 **bits**; the colours are what those bits can distinguish.

questions.prompt: A sound is sampled at 4000 Hz with a sample resolution of 8 bits for 5 seconds. What is the file size in bits?
An image is 100 pixels wide and 50 pixels high with a colour depth of 8 bits. What is its file size in bytes?
questions.solution: $100 \times 50 \times 8 = 40\,000$ bits, and $40\,000 \div 8 = $ **5000** bytes. The formula gives bits, so the divide by 8 is essential.

questions.prompt: Complete the specification's definition: a sample is a measure of ______ at a point in time.
questions.solution: A measure of **amplitude** at a point in time — the height of the sound wave at that instant.

questions.prompt: What unit is sampling rate measured in?
options: Hertz
Bits
Bytes per second
Decibels
questions.solution: **Hertz (Hz)**, where 1 hertz is 1 sample per second. Bits are the unit of sample **resolution**.

questions.prompt: A black and white bitmap is 8 pixels wide and 8 pixels high with a colour depth of 1 bit. How many bits are needed to store it?
questions.solution: $8 \times 8 \times 1 = $ **64** bits — one bit for each of the 64 pixels.

questions.prompt: Why must sound be converted before a computer can store it?
options: Sound is analogue and continuous, but a computer stores discrete values
Sound travels too quickly to be recorded directly
Sound is already digital but in the wrong format
Computers can only store images, not sound
questions.solution: A sound wave is **analogue** — it varies continuously and has a value at every instant. A computer stores **discrete** binary numbers, so the wave must be sampled at intervals and each measurement stored as a number.

markScheme.description: sound is analogue, computers store discrete values

questions.prompt: An image's width and height are both doubled, with the colour depth unchanged. What happens to its file size?
options: It becomes four times as large
It becomes twice as large
It becomes eight times as large
It stays the same, as the depth is unchanged
questions.solution: Both $W$ and $H$ appear in $W \times H \times D$, so doubling each multiplies the size by $2 \times 2 = $ **4**. Answering "twice" means only one of the two dimensions has been counted.

questions.prompt: A question says an image uses 256 colours. What value goes into the file size formula as D?
options: 8, because 256 colours needs 8 bits per pixel
256, because that is the colour depth given
2, because there are two states per bit
32, because 256 divided by 8 is 32
questions.solution: $D$ is the **bits per pixel**, and $2^8 = 256$, so $D = $ **8**. Putting 256 into the formula makes the answer 32 times too large — a very visible error, and a common one.

questions.prompt: A sound is sampled at 8000 Hz with 8-bit resolution for 10 seconds. What is the file size in kilobytes?
questions.solution: $8000 \times 8 \times 10 = 640\,000$ bits. Divide by 8: $80\,000$ bytes. Divide by 1000: **80** kB. Both divisions are needed, and the second uses 1 kB = 1000 bytes.

questions.prompt: Why can a digital recording never be an exact copy of the original sound?
options: Nothing is recorded between one sample and the next
Binary cannot represent the loudness of a sound
The microphone always adds errors to every sample
Sound files are always compressed when saved
questions.solution: The original wave is **continuous**, with a value at every instant. Sampling records it only at **intervals**, and whatever the wave did between two samples is never stored. Raising the sampling rate makes the approximation closer but never exact.

questions.prompt: The same 16 bits of a 1-bit bitmap are read as 2 pixels wide instead of 4. What happens?
options: A different image appears, because the rows break in different places
The image is identical but rotated by ninety degrees
Only half of the image can be displayed
Nothing changes, as the same bits are stored
questions.solution: The bits are the same but the **rows break in different places**, so the picture is completely different: 16 bits make a 4 × 4 image or an 8 × 2 one. This is why the width must be known, and why checking the bit count against $W \times H \times D$ is worth doing.

markScheme.description: a different image, as the rows break differently

questions.prompt: Two recordings of the same sound have the same duration and sampling rate, but one has twice the sample resolution. What is true?
options: It is twice the size, and each amplitude is recorded more precisely
It is twice the size, and twice as many samples are taken
It is the same size, as only the rate affects file size
It is four times the size, as resolution is squared
questions.solution: Resolution is a **linear** factor in rate × res × secs, so doubling it **doubles** the file. It changes how precisely each amplitude is recorded, not **how many** samples are taken — that is the sampling **rate**, which is unchanged here.

markScheme.description: twice the size, more precise amplitudes

questions.prompt: Explain how a bitmap image is represented, and describe how the number of pixels and the colour depth affect the file size and the quality.
questions.solution:
A **pixel** — short for **picture element** — is a **single point** in an image. A bitmap image is a grid of pixels, and the computer stores a binary code for each one recording its colour. There is nothing else in a bitmap: no shapes or lines, just the colour of every point, which is why zooming far enough into one shows the squares.

Two properties describe it. **Image size** is measured **in pixels**, written **width × height**, so a 100 × 50 image holds 5,000 pixels. **Colour depth** is the number of **bits used to represent each pixel**. It is a count of bits, not of colours: the number of colours available is $2^D$, so a depth of 1 bit gives 2 colours, 8 bits gives 256, and 24 bits gives over 16 million.

**The file size formula** given in the specification is:

$$\text{Size (bits)} = W \times H \times D \qquad \text{Size (bytes)} = \frac{W \times H \times D}{8}$$

For an image 100 pixels wide and 50 high at 8-bit depth: $100 \times 50 \times 8 = 40\,000$ bits, which is $40\,000 \div 8 = 5\,000$ bytes, or **5 kB**. The formula produces **bits**, so the division by 8 is essential whenever bytes are asked for — leaving the answer in bits is the commonest way to lose the final mark.

**Both factors increase the file size**, because every pixel is stored and every pixel costs the same number of bits. More pixels means more of them; a greater colour depth means each one is more expensive. Both act **linearly**, so doubling the colour depth doubles the file. Doubling **both** the width and the height multiplies it by **four**, since both appear in the formula — a point worth making in this form rather than by recalculating.

**Both also improve quality.** More pixels give more detail, because the image is sampled at more points; too few and it looks blocky, with the individual squares visible. A greater colour depth allows finer shading between similar colours; too little and a smooth gradient, such as a sky, breaks into visible bands.

So the choice is a trade-off. Higher values give a better image and a larger file, and the right setting depends on what the image is for — a photograph to be printed needs far more of both than an icon on a web page.

questions.prompt: Explain how sound is represented digitally, and explain why a digital recording is always an approximation of the original.
questions.solution:
**Sound is analogue.** A real sound wave varies **continuously**: it has a value at every instant and those values change smoothly. A computer can only store **discrete** binary numbers, so the wave has to be converted into a digital form before it can be stored or processed.

That conversion is **sampling**. The height of the wave is measured at regular intervals and each measurement is stored as a binary number. The specification defines a **sample** as **a measure of amplitude at a point in time** — the height of the wave at that instant.

Two properties describe the result. **Sampling rate** is the **number of samples taken in one second**, measured in **hertz**, where 1 Hz is one sample per second. **Sample resolution** is the **number of bits used for each sample**; more bits allow each amplitude to be recorded more precisely.

The file size follows from multiplying everything involved:

$$\text{File size (bits)} = \text{rate} \times \text{res} \times \text{secs}$$

A recording at 8,000 Hz with 8-bit resolution for 10 seconds is $8000 \times 8 \times 10 = 640\,000$ bits, which is 80,000 bytes, or **80 kB**. Each of the three factors is **linear**, so doubling the rate, the resolution or the duration doubles the file — and raising the rate and the resolution together raises quality and size at the same time.

**The digital version can never be exact**, and the reason is in the method itself. The original wave is **continuous**, so it has a value at every one of infinitely many instants. Sampling records it only at **intervals**, and whatever the wave did **between** two samples is never captured — the computer simply has no record of it, and reconstructing the sound means assuming something about the gap.

The **resolution** adds a second approximation. Each amplitude must be rounded to one of the $2^{res}$ values the available bits can express, so even the samples that were taken are stored slightly wrong.

Raising either setting reduces the error. A higher rate leaves smaller gaps; a higher resolution makes each stored value closer to the true one. But neither closes the gap entirely, because a continuous wave cannot be captured by a finite number of measurements however many are taken. The digital recording is an **approximation** that can be made as close as is worth paying for in file size — which is exactly the trade-off that decides settings such as CD quality.

examTechnique.body:
Write the formula first: **W × H × D** for an image, **rate × res × secs** for sound. Both give **bits** — divide by **8** for bytes and again by **1000** for kilobytes.

Colour depth is **bits per pixel**; the number of colours is $2^D$. Reason about changes linearly: doubling **both** image dimensions gives **×4**.
examinerErrors: Leaving the answer in bits when bytes were asked for.
Substituting the number of colours for the colour depth.
Saying doubling both dimensions doubles the file size.
Confusing sampling rate with sample resolution.
Defining a sample as "a bit of the sound".
Explaining lossy sound as "the quality drops" with no reason.
Adding an allowance for a file header, which is not wanted.
Drawing a bitmap without checking the bit count against W × H × D.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer writes **W × H × D** or **rate × res × secs** before substituting, and converts to the unit the question actually asked for. It keeps **colour depth** (bits) apart from the **number of colours** ($2^D$), and reasons about change linearly — *four times, because both dimensions are in the formula* — rather than recalculating. It uses the specification's wording, **a measure of amplitude at a point in time**, and explains approximation from the method: the wave is **continuous**, sampling records only **intervals**, and each sample is additionally **rounded** to the available bits. It says a higher rate gets closer without ever being exact.
